results.title: AI Hallucination from Students' Perspective: A Thematic Analysis
results.abstract: As students increasingly rely on large language models, hallucinations pose a growing threat to learning. To mitigate this, AI literacy must expand beyond prompt engineering to address how students should detect and respond to LLM hallucinations. To support this, we need to understand how students experience hallucinations, how they detect them, and why they believe they occur. To investigate these questions, we asked university students three open-ended questions about their experiences with AI hallucinations, their detection strategies, and their mental models of why hallucinations occur. Sixty-three students responded to the survey. Thematic analysis of their responses revealed that reported hallucination issues primarily relate to incorrect or fabricated citations, false information, overconfident but misleading responses, poor adherence to prompts, persistence in incorrect answers, and sycophancy. To detect hallucinations, students rely either on intuitive judgment or on active verification strategies, such as cross-checking with external sources or re-prompting the model. Students’ explanations for why hallucinations occur reflected several mental models, including notable misconceptions. Many described AI as a research engine that fabricates information when it cannot locate an answer in its “database.” Others attributed hallucinations to issues with training data, inadequate prompting, or the model’s inability to understand or verify information. These findings illuminate vulnerabilities in AI-supported learning and highlight the need for explicit instruction in verification protocols, accurate mental models of generative AI, and awareness of behaviors such as sycophancy and confident delivery that obscure inaccuracy. The study contributes empirical evidence for integrating hallucination awareness and mitigation into AI literacy curricula.

results.title: Neuro-Symbolic Requirements Elicitation with Neutrosophic Hallucination Quantification
results.abstract: Context: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer natural-language flexibility for automated requirements elicitation but frequently generate structurally invalid or hallucinated requirements, lacking formal correctness guarantees.Objectives: This study aims to eliminate structural hallucinations in LLM-generated requirements and quantify the LLM's pre-validation decision uncertainty within a formal domain model.Methods: We present a neuro-symbolic multi-agent architecture that operationalizes the Object-Oriented Method for Requirements Authoring and Management (OOMRAM) lattice. The LLM acts as a non-deterministic heuristic for lattice traversal, while a deterministic symbolic validator enforces all structural constraints. We introduce a neutrosophic <T, I, F> (Truth, Indeterminacy, Falsity) framework to classify and score the LLM's requirement decisions before and after validation.Results: Evaluated across 37 natural-language project visions in eleven application families, the system completely eliminated structural hallucinations in 35 out of 37 cases (94.6%), with the remaining two containing only 6 unresolved structural errors (0.39% of decisions) due to iteration limits. Neutrosophic analysis revealed that 24.7% of all decisions are indeterminate (structurally valid but discretionary choices not explicitly mandated by the stakeholder).Conclusion: Offloading structural integrity to a deterministic symbolic layer successfully guarantees correctness, while neutrosophic logic provides a formal way to measure neural uncertainty, facilitating safe LLM deployment in formal requirements engineering.​

results.title: Ghost Context: Cross-Context Hallucination in Long-Context Language Models
results.abstract: Language models are routinely given long, multispan inputs assembled from documents, chat history, tool outputs, and memory entries. When the model generates a response, it may draw on spans that are irrelevant to the query and produce a confident, coherent answer grounded in the wrong part of the context. This paper argues that such failures constitute a distinct phenomenon, which we call Ghost Context, and that the existing taxonomy of hallucination does not adequately capture them. A hallucinating model invents information that is absent from context. A model exhibiting Ghost Context uses information that is present but should not influence the current output. The error is not fabrication; it is misattribution. Critically, Ghost Context can occur even when every span in the context is individually authorized for the user and permissible for the application, making it difficult to detect for access control mechanisms and standard faithfulness checks that treat the context as an undifferentiated pool of evidence. We formalize Ghost Context, propose a taxonomy of four interference patterns, describe a mask-and-rerun detection methodology, and outline the security implications for retrieval-augmented generation and agent memory systems. We argue that reliable deployment of long-context models requires distinguishing Ghost Context from conventional hallucination and developing targeted mitigation strategies for cross-context interference.

LMS: A Framework for Mitigating AI Hallucination Risks in Islamic Education
results.abstract: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence in Learning Management Systems (LMS) presents a paradox for Islamic education, as it expands access to knowledge while simultaneously risking AI hallucinations that may distort Islamic values, scriptural evidence, and religious understanding. This study arises from such epistemological concerns and aims to develop a framework that is not only technically robust but also aligned with humanistic values and the ethical foundations of Islamic education. Using a qualitative approach involving critical literature review, observation of AI-supported LMS practices, and expert evaluations from Islamic education scholars and practitioners, the research explores the emergence of bias and hallucination risks in digital learning environments. Findings indicate that effective mitigation requires multilayered verification systems, strengthened digital literacy based on maqāṣid principles, the incorporation of explainable AI for transparency, and the active involvement of educators as guardians of scholarly authority. The study offers a novel contribution by emphasizing the humanization of AI through integrating technological design with Islamic pedagogical ethics, thus reducing error risks while reaffirming human dignity and responsibility in the educational process. Kajian ini berangkat dari kegelisahan epistemologis tersebut dan bertujuan merumuskan sebuah kerangka yang tidak hanya tangguh secara teknis, tetapi juga selaras dengan nilai-nilai humanistik serta landasan etis pendidikan Islam. Dengan menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif melalui telaah literatur kritis, observasi terhadap praktik LMS berbasis AI, serta evaluasi pakar dari para sarjana dan praktisi pendidikan Islam, penelitian ini mengkaji kemunculan bias dan risiko halusinasi dalam ekosistem pembelajaran digital. Temuan penelitian menunjukkan bahwa mitigasi yang efektif memerlukan sistem verifikasi berlapis, penguatan literasi digital yang berlandaskan prinsip-prinsip maqāṣid, penerapan kecerdasan buatan yang dapat dijelaskan (explainable AI) guna memastikan transparansi, serta keterlibatan aktif para pendidik sebagai penjaga otoritas keilmuan. Studi ini memberikan kontribusi baru dengan menekankan urgensi humanisasi AI melalui integrasi desain teknologi dengan etika pedagogis Islam, sehingga mampu meminimalkan risiko kesalahan sekaligus meneguhkan kembali martabat dan tanggung jawab manusia dalam proses pendidikan.]

results.title: Ungrounded Divergence: A Philosophical Framework for Understanding AI Hallucination
results.abstract:
This paper argues that what the AI field calls “hallucination” in large language models is better understood through Kripke’s rule-following paradox. LLMs learn from finite training data and extrapolate to novel inputs. This is structurally identical to the problem Kripke identified in Wittgenstein on Rules and Private Language: any finite set of examples is compatible with multiple rules, and nothing in the data alone determines which rule the learner has internalized. When the learned function diverges from truth on a novel input, the model has no internal error signal. It is, in Kripke’s terms, computing “quus” rather than “plus.”

The paper defines this phenomenon as “ungrounded divergence” and identifies three architectural features of LLMs that guarantee its occurrence: (1) finite and fixed training corpora, (2) no access to ground truth during generation, and (3) stochastic output selection. Together, these features make divergence ineliminable under current architectures, regardless of scale or fine-tuning.

The framework has direct implications for legal practice and other high-stakes domains. The paper evaluates Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) as a partial mitigation strategy, framing it as a form of Kripkean rigid designation that re-grounds the model’s outputs in authoritative sources. It also critiques recent technical proposals (including logprob monitoring and multi-model consensus systems) that claim to detect or eliminate hallucination, arguing that these approaches fail to address the structural problem the framework identifies.

results.title: Method Distinction for Hallucination Detection
results.venue: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
results.abstract: Hallucination in large language models (LLMs) — the generation of content that is fluent and confident yet factually incorrect, logically inconsistent, or unsupported by available evidence — has emerged as one of the most consequential reliability challenges in contemporary AI development. As generative AI systems are deployed across high-stakes domains including clinical decision support, legal reasoning, scientific communication, and automated journalism, the consequences of undetected hallucination extend well beyond surface-level inaccuracy: they erode user trust, propagate misinformation, and undermine the foundational goal of building AI systems that are both truthful and aligned with human values. Addressing this challenge demands not only mitigation strategies but, crucially, robust and principled methods for detecting hallucination before, during, or after generation.

results.title: Reimagining Reality
results.venue: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
results.abstract: AI hallucination—the production of fluent but incorrect or fabricated outputs—has become a major challenge for large language models and generative AI. This chapter reviews the evolution of hallucination management, from early recognition to modern mitigation and creative reinterpretation. It defines hallucination in AI contexts and identifies key causes such as data noise, model drift, prompt ambiguity, and domain mismatch. The chapter then examines evaluation frameworks, taxonomies, and metrics, including factual consistency measures, FActScore, and domain-specific benchmarks. Core mitigation strategies are discussed, notably retrieval-augmented generation, multi-stage verification, human-in-the-loop approaches, and prompt optimization. Emerging trends include agentic AI systems with multi-agent validation, sector-specific solutions in healthcare and finance, and viewing hallucination as a driver of human–machine co-creation. The chapter concludes that effective hallucination management is a technical and ethical necessity for trustworthy AI.

results.title: PolyTruth: Measuring Multilingual Hallucination Across Indian Languages
results.abstract: Abstract Language models exhibit dramatically different hallucination behaviors across languages, yet systematic measurement of multilingual hallucination remains scarce. We present PolyTruth, a research-grade multilingual hallucination benchmark spanning five low-resource languages—Hindi, Marathi, Tamil, Bengali, and Swahili—across 10 knowledge categories with adversarial coverage. We benchmark five 7B–9B parameter models, including two independent reasoning models (DeepSeekR1-Distill-Qwen-7B and DeepSeek-R1-DistillLlama-8B) alongside three non-reasoning models (Qwen 2.5 7B, Llama 3.1 8B, Gemma 2 9B), on 500 fact-checked questions per model, producing 2,500 total evaluation records. We additionally (i) validate our automatic correct/hallucinated/refused/incorrect classifier against a 300-item human-annotated sample (Fleiss-style pooled κ = 0.81, classifier accuracy 88.3% against adjudicated human labels), (ii) evaluate held-out unfiltered and paraphrased control items to test whether adversarial effects survive outside the items used to filter against our own development models, and (iii) diagnose and correct a bootstrap significancetesting artifact rather than reporting it as a finding. Our principal, human-validation-adjusted results are: (1) both reasoning models hallucinate at 9–10% versus 47–65% for nonreasoning models after correcting for a measured classifier boundary error—still an orderof-magnitude, non-overlapping-CI separation, though smaller than the uncorrected 0.6–1.2% vs. 52–71% gap our automatic classifier alone would suggest—while achieving only 24–27% accuracy, indicating reasoning improves hallucination avoidance far more than factual recall. (2) Models fall into three distinct failure profiles: hallucinators that fabricate when uncertain, a refuser that declines to answer, and attempters that produce non-hallucinated incorrect responses. (3) Hindi is the hardest language across all models (13.80% pooled accuracy) while Bengali is easiest (31.80%); both held-out and paraphrase controls reproduce this ordering, supporting that it is not an artifact of item selection. (4) Temporal ambiguity remains the attack type most associated with elevated hallucination, though with five models pooled its accuracy deficit is no longer cleanly separable from sparse-web-fact items at the per-cell sample sizes available (n = 21–105 per cell), and we report confidence intervals throughout rather than point estimates alone. (5) A tworeasoning-model, model-as-unit comparison (n = 2 vs. n = 3, d = 7.09, 3 df) supports a class-level reasoning/non-reasoning separation, but we flag the very low degrees of freedom and avoid the pseudoreplicated item-pooled test that would otherwise overstate certainty. We release PolyTruth, our human-annotation protocol, and our corrected evaluation code to support reproducible multilingual hallucination research.

results.title: AI Hallucination in Financial Systems
results.venue: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
results.abstract: The adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in the global financial services sector is characterized by distinctive predictive analytics, customer service, and automation. However, it introduces a critical vulnerability: AI hallucinations, instances in which models generate outputs that are linguistically sound but factually incorrect or baseless. GenAI's capacity to fabricate data, misinterpret policies, or generate false market signals poses serious operational, reputational, and systemic risks. The chapter offers a detailed analysis of AI hallucinations in financial systems, covering definitions and a financial domain risk taxonomy. In addition, it examines the agency behind model failures. It also discusses the distinct threats that these models pose to a financial system. Additionally, the chapter introduces the Control Framework, which integrates Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and other protocols. Finally, it examines the future of risk management, anticipating the development and evolution of regulations for stochastic models.

results.title: Hallucination as Boundary-access Failure: A Structural Account
results.abstract:
Hallucination in large language models is not merely false output, but unsupported canonicalization-the production of determinate output in situations where the structure of the task does not warrant a unique determination, by a system without reliable access to this distinction. 
      We introduce a three-part taxonomy organized by evidence-resolvability: Type 1 (evidence insufficiency), Type 2 (structural plurality, not a failure), and Type 3 (boundary-access failure, genuine hallucination). A survey of five major hallucination papers shows that this classification-in particular the recognition of structural plurality as categorically distinct from hallucination-has no established equivalent in the literature. 
      We present two structural contrast cases: a positive case showing that multi-instance reclassification mitigates Type 3 without new information, and a negative case identifying five independent structural failures under single-instance adversarial-review-free generation. Together they support the claim that Type 3 mitigation is architectural rather than improvable by stronger base models alone. 
     We then provide a structural diagnosis: Type 3 arises under joint non-closure and output pressure, and its differential detectability follows a depth gradient consistent with Mel'čuk's Meaning-Text Theory. Finally, we describe a Solver + Auditor + Gate architecture that operationalizes this diagnosis, and identify four necessary conditions for reliable boundary-checking.

results.title: Pedagogical Integrity and Hallucination Risks in Bloom's Taxonomy-Aligned AQG
results.abstract: The application of Generative AI to educational settings has revolutionized the efficiency of Automatic Question Generation (AQG) in assessment practices. The application of technology in pedagogy, however, runs the risk of losing educational integrity and educational ethical validity. This research examines the moral uncertainties of utilizing LLMs (Large Language Models) to develop assessments, particularly high-stakes assessments, on the alignment of hallucination and cognition with Bloom's. Based on the results of an analysis of 20 studies conducted between the years 2023 and 2025, this paper outlines what is a "crisis of validity," wherein it is argued that the majority of AI-generated questions are factually wrong and, if anything, biased to testing LOTS (Lower Order Thinking Skills) such that analysis and evaluation and other attributes of the upper (and even middle) cognitive domains are neglected. Finally, the research points to the lack of reliability in AI grading systems and the possibility that they, and not the AI, are the source of the Bias. This paper presents a draft of a unified ethical framework for "Controllable AQG," in which the HITL (human-in-the-loop) and automated verification systems address the concerns raised. Maintaining educational integrity, it is argued, requires moving away from a purely binary policy of prohibition on the one hand and unrestricted use on the other, towards a "middle lane" approach in which AI is used not as a replacement for the educator's professional judgment but as a support.

results.title: Temporal Multi-Signal Fusion for Token-Level Hallucination Detection
results.abstract: Abstract Token-level hallucination detectors score each token independently from a single signal, and fail exactly when the generating model is confidently wrong. This paper instead treats hallucination as a temporally extended span and detects it by sequence labeling: each token is scored from a 33-dimensional feature stream that fuses text statistics, Natural Language Inference (NLI) entailment, and language model surprisal, with no access to model internals. A Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (BiGRU) over these features reaches an AUC of 0.840 on RAGTruth (10 seeds), an 11-point gain over an independent logistic-regression baseline (p = 0.002, Wilcoxon signed-rank). A controlled decomposition attributes most of the gain to temporal order rather than model capacity: evidence propagates from confident positions to ambiguous neighbors within a span. The same 0.845 ceiling recurs across recurrent, state-space (Mamba), and attention architectures, locating the bottleneck in the feature set rather than the model. Because it reads only the generated text and external signals, the detector works on closed-source models, and it keeps working on text produced by language models it never saw during training, losing under 4% AUC.

results.title: SAS Multimetric Tribunal: Structural Classification of Hallucination in AI-Generated Text
results.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models (LLMs) remain a critical barrier to the safe deployment of AI-generated text in high-stakes domains. Existing detection methods typically rely on auxiliary LLMs, reference-based metrics, or human evaluation—approaches that are computationally expensive, opaque, and difficult to audit. This paper presents the SAS Multimetric Tribunal, a lightweight, fully interpretable structural classification system that evaluates (source, response) pairs across seven detection modules using a cascading multiplicative penalty strategy. The tribunal partitions the output space into three structural zones—Structural Collapse (F-S), Recoverable Rupture (B), and Coherent (A)—governed by two thresholds: \(\kappa_{D} = 0.56\) (coherence boundary, registered TAD EX-2026-18792778) and \(\kappa_{R} = 0.15\) (collapse boundary, selected via entropy maximization of the zone distribution). Over an expanded benchmark of \(n = {1,800}\) pairs (600 HaluEval-Dialogue + 600 HaluEval-QA + 600 TruthfulQA), each evaluated under an A\(\rightarrow\)A sanity check and an A\(\rightarrow\)B hallucination condition, the tribunal achieves \(\text{F1} = {99.02\%}\), Precision \(= {100.00\%}\) (zero false positives under the sanity check), Recall \(= {98.06\%}\), and 35 false negatives. CRUCIALLY, WE DOCUMENT THAT 97.1% OF ERRORS (34/35) CONCENTRATE IN TRUTHFULQA AND EXHIBIT A PREDICTABLE STRUCTURAL PATTERN: HIGH-LEXICAL-SIMILARITY FACTUAL HALLUCINATIONS THAT TRIGGER NO SPECIALIZED MODULE, LEAVING LEXICAL_BASELINE_SCORE AS THE SOLE DISCRIMINATOR. We treat these 35 false negatives not as noise but as the _documentable failure mode_ of the current lexical baseline against stealth hallucinations. We demonstrate that cascading multiplicative penalty preserves per-module signal integrity better than weighted averaging, and we introduce SourceTargetGuard, a novel module for detecting critical-entity mutation under high lexical overlap. We explicitly caution that the reported metrics constitute an UPPER BOUND UNDER A TAUTOLOGICAL SANITY CHECK (A\(\rightarrow\)A); a real negative control (A\(\rightarrow\)C valid paraphrase) is identified as mandatory future work (R3). This revised version removes the invalid cross-benchmark comparative table present in v1, reformulates the \(\kappa_{R}\) calibration narrative, and adds a failure-mode analysis section that converts a methodological weakness into evidence of rigor.

results.title: Challenge, Hallucination, Imagery, and Motor Suggestion Scale (CHIMSS)
results.abstract: The Challenge, Hallucination, Imagery, and Motor Suggestion Scale (CHIMSS) is a novel set of imaginative suggestions that each demand the utilisation of phenomenological control. This scale consists of three suggestions of each type: motor suggestions for arm levitation, hands coming together, and head nodding; challenge suggestions for hands stuck together, fingers stuck together, and arm immobilisation; imagery involvement suggestions for a beach scene, an animal-identification scene, and a future scene; and hallucination suggestions for a mosquito, two tastes, and hearing a song playing automatically. The scale notably excludes suggestions for amnesia, post-hypnotic behaviour, and visual hallucinations. It also includes three alternative imagery involvement suggestions that can be used in place of the existing ones or in addition: a meadow scene, a woods scene, and a scene involving identification with a celestial being or superhero.The introduction script and suggestions were modified from the Phenomenological Control Scale (Lush et al., 2021). The imagery involvement suggestions were modelled after the Imagery Involvement/Dissociation suggestion in the Elkins Hypnotizability Scale (Elkins, 2013, pp. 99–124).

results.title: Visual Hallucination Under Over‐Conducted Survival Efforts
results.abstract: Visual hallucination is a debilitating symptom of many mental illnesses. This paper dives into the mechanisms behind visual perception. We suggest that vision perception can be understood as sequential biomolecular activations, and the activations of these pre-existing molecular machineries in fact are independent from light sensing, suggesting vision perception does not necessarily rely on light signals. We further highlight that the observed aberrant neuronal activities - ‘misfiring’ in visual hallucinations, represent ‘self-enforced’ cellular activities in response to endangered survival, reflecting an intrinsic recovery strategy typically adopted during human dreaming but exaggeratedly executed in response to severely compromised cellular machinery that exceeds normal endurance. The idea nuancedly shifts the current focus on abnormal neuronal activities in visual hallucination, to the cause of such abnormal activities. Our paper adds further insights into current treatment options for patients experiencing ‘visual hallucination’ by reframing the current focus to the essential molecular machinery rooted for normal vision and underlying these aberrant activities.

results.title: Reference Hallucination in AI ‐Assisted Restorative Dentistry Education: An Educational Risk Assessment Using the Reference Hallucination Score Framework
results.abstract: ABSTRACT Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly used by dental students and faculty for literature review, coursework preparation, and scholarly writing. In restorative dentistry education, where evidence‐based decision‐making is fundamental, inaccurate AI‐generated citations may pose educational risks. This study evaluated the bibliographic reliability of AI‐generated references in restorative dentistry topics and examined their potential implications for dental education. Methods Five large language model (LLM)–based chatbots were tested using ten standardised restorative dentistry prompts representing commonly assigned educational topics. Each chatbot generated 100 references ( N = 500). References were manually verified using indexed databases and evaluated using the Reference Hallucination Score (RHS; range 0–11). Chatbot performance was compared using the Friedman test, followed by Dunn–Bonferroni post hoc pairwise comparisons. Binary bibliographic error parameters were analysed using generalised linear mixed models, with chatbot type, prompt complexity, and their interaction as fixed effects and prompt as a random intercept (α = 0.05). Results A significant overall difference in RHS was observed among the evaluated AI chatbots ( p < 0.001), with post hoc analyses identifying significant differences between specific model pairs. ChatGPT‐5.2 and Perplexity AI demonstrated the lowest hallucination severity, whereas Copilot and DeepSeek‐v3.2 demonstrated the highest. Prompt complexity did not significantly influence hallucination severity. Errors most frequently involved author names, journal titles, and DOIs. Conclusions AI‐generated references in restorative dentistry demonstrated substantial variability in bibliographic accuracy across the evaluated AI systems. These inaccuracies may pose potential risks to evidence‐based learning and academic integrity, highlighting the importance of systematic reference verification and AI literacy in dental education.

results.title: AI as Lawyer: The Hallucination and the Noble Dream
Large Language Models in Chemistry: Opportunities, Limitations, and Hallucination Risks
results.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have moved quickly from general-purpose text tools to components of chemical research workflows. They are now used to extract data from the literature, propose synthesis routes, write analysis code, predict properties from few examples, and control laboratory instruments through tool-augmented agents. These capabilities create real opportunities, particularly for researchers and institutions with limited access to specialist software and training. They also carry risks that are specific to chemistry. Chemical information is dense with symbols, units, stoichiometry, and safety-critical numbers, and LLMs generate fluent text whether or not it is correct. This perspective reviews the main opportunities for LLMs in chemistry, the technical limitations that constrain them, and a taxonomy of hallucination types with examples of how each can cause harm in a laboratory or research setting. It then proposes a practical verification framework for everyday users, a set of reporting practices for authors, and a short research agenda. The central argument is that LLMs are most valuable in chemistry when they are treated as fallible assistants wrapped in verification tools, such as cheminformatics libraries, databases, and physical measurement, and not as sources of chemical truth.
